title: Under Symmetric Label Noise, Most Out-of-Fold Disagreements of Logistic Regression Are Mislabeled Samples
insight: On two small datasets with symmetric label noise, a training label that logistic regression contradicts out of fold is usually wrong, and this single check catches most of the wrong labels.
abstract_sketch: When training labels are flipped at random to other classes, most samples whose label logistic regression contradicts out of fold are truly mislabeled, and they include most of the flipped labels. We measure this against the known flips on two small datasets at two noise rates, using a one-pass filter that drops every disagreeing sample and refits on the rest, with no clean validation set, noise-rate estimate, or confidence threshold. The refit is more accurate than training on all noisy labels on digits at both rates and on breast cancer at the higher rate, while on breast cancer at the lower rate its mean is higher but five seeds do not establish the difference. With clean labels every dropped sample is correctly labeled, yet mean test accuracy falls by only a fraction of a point. Under noise the filter also discards correct samples and does not restore clean-label accuracy, winning back only a small part of the loss on breast cancer at the higher rate.
figure1: A full-width teaser at the top of page 1 that reads without the text. (a) Schematic, 'Check each label': a stack of training cards with given labels, a few marked as flipped, passes through three numbered stages (Predict out of fold, Drop mismatches, Refit); the dropped pile holds mostly flipped cards plus one correct card, and the caption calls the cards schematic. (b) Measured, 'What gets dropped': for each dataset with clean labels and at both noise rates, a stacked bar shows the share of the training set removed, split into mislabeled samples (accent color) and correctly labeled samples (light accent), with a tick at the share of the whole training set that was flipped. On noisy sets the mislabeled segment fills most of each bar (drop precision) and covers most of the height to the tick (drop recall), while the small clean-label bars hold only correct samples. (c) Measured, 'What the refit returns': grouped bars of clean-label test accuracy for our filter and for logistic regression trained on the same labels, a gray line for logistic regression trained on clean labels, and seed points paired by thin lines, so the usual gain, the one losing noisy run, the remaining gap, and the wide spread and small recovery on breast cancer at the higher rate are all visible. The caption gives the number of seeds and states that error bars are standard deviations.
contributions: We describe a one-pass filter that drops every training sample whose out-of-fold logistic regression prediction disagrees with its given label and refits on the rest, with no clean validation set, noise-rate estimate, or confidence threshold.
We show that on noisy training sets most dropped samples are truly mislabeled and most flipped labels are dropped, on both of our datasets and at both symmetric noise rates.
We measure what the refit gains and costs: it beats training on all noisy labels in all but one noisy run and costs little with clean labels, but it does not restore clean-label accuracy.
storyline: Symmetric label noise lowers the accuracy of logistic regression, more at the higher rate, and the filter we study has no clean set or noise rate to tell it which labels to distrust. Disagreement with an out-of-fold prediction turns out to be an informative cue: in every noisy setting, most disagreeing samples are mislabeled and most flipped labels are among them. Each sample is judged by a model that never trained on it, so one pass can check every given label, drop the mismatches, and refit without a confidence threshold. The refit beats training on all noisy labels in all but one noisy run, with the difference established on digits at both rates and on breast cancer at the higher rate, and it costs little with clean labels. The cue is imperfect: the filter discards correct samples, misses more flips under heavier noise, leaves a gap to clean-label accuracy, and wins back only a small part of the loss on breast cancer at the higher rate. Reporting the dropped set beside the accuracy lets a reader judge a disagreement filter by what it removes and by what that returns.

sections.title: Method: One Pass of Out-of-Fold Filtering
Most dropped samples are mislabeled and most flips are caught, but correct samples go too
Refitting usually helps under noise and costs little on clean labels, but recovery is partial
Plain logistic regression also beats the MLP under noise, so our lead over it does not isolate filtering

risks: The first attack is the missing random-drop and oracle controls: the accuracy gain could come from removing samples at all. The paper does not attribute the gain to the choice of samples. It scores the selection directly against the known flips, where the mislabeled share of the dropped set is far higher than that of the whole training set, and it states that whether the refit needs this selectivity is untested. The second attack is novelty, since the filter is close to classification filtering and confident learning: the paper claims no new method and no advantage over methods it did not run, and offers a measured account of what one pass removes and returns. The third is scale: two small datasets, synthetic symmetric noise at two rates, one setting of folds and regularization, and five seeds that re-split the same data, so tests are read as descriptive, every setting is shown, and the exceptions are named. The fourth is that the headline finding reverses with clean labels, where every drop is a correct sample; the paper reports this beside the finding and in Fig. 1. The last is the MLP comparison, which the paper presents as noise sensitivity of one untuned model and not as a benefit of filtering.
